title: Some plans end on a rock. Ours started there.
lede: The story of Eagle Ray Expeditions, from seven boats to La Paz.

seo.title: Our story — Eagle Ray Expeditions
seo.description: From seven boats to La Paz: how Eagle Ray Expeditions started, and why every trip is designed around the people on board.

body:
## Thibault Poirson wanted to sail the Atlantic to the Caribbean. Getting there took seven boats.

On EOS, an Amel Maramu, he learned that a plan is only as good as the people ready to follow it. On Tawhiri, a Dufour 360 in Brittany, a skipper named Zach showed him that the best captains teach while they steer. Silver Kiss, a catamaran shared with a group of friends, made the gap obvious: finding a boat is easy, designing a trip around the people on it is not. Najida took him offshore, away from signal and schedule. Adventure, sailing the Canary Islands with a young crew, showed how quickly good energy falls apart without structure. Blue Challenge took months of searching for the right boat, dates, captain and crew before leaving with Baris as skipper.


The seventh was Enola, a seventy-foot aluminum expedition yacht. A few days from Cabo Verde, she hit a rock, and the crossing ended there.
Thibault never reached the Caribbean. He came back with a clear idea of what makes time at sea work for the people on board, and of how rarely anyone designs a trip around it.

![Thibault Poirson, founder of Eagle Ray Expeditions](/assets/img/founder-thibault.webp)

> That idea became Eagle Ray Expeditions. We offer private time at sea with the people you choose to bring.

Our crew runs the boat and keeps everyone safe, so each day can follow what the group actually wants: diving in, learning to read the wind, changing the plan because something showed up, or doing nothing at all. The sailboat is how we get there. It was never the point.

## How we work

Most charters start with the boat. We start the other way around: first the group and what they want from their days at sea, then the crew who fits them, and only then the boat.

We sail with private groups only. Nobody shares the deck with strangers, and nobody is fitted into someone else's schedule.

And we're honest about the sea. The Sea of Cortez decides a lot of things: the wind, the water, which bay is calm tomorrow. When it does, we say so and change the route. Some of the best days on board were never in the plan.
